title: Winter and Portrait
premise: Isandro Ravensworth hosts a late-night call-in show, but tonight every caller is someone who died within the past week — and they all mention the same sealed door unearthed beneath the old Ravensworth estate. As he documents their voices, he learns the door was locked from the inside by his great-grandmother to contain something the family invited in generations ago, a bargain paid in identities: each generation surrenders one member's face and name to feed what waits. When the excavation crew breaches the seal, the thing pours out wearing stolen faces, including Isandro's own. To survive until sunrise, Isandro must choose between erasing himself from every record — becoming no one, uninvited — or letting it wear him forever; he chooses oblivion, and at dawn a stranger's voice signs off the show that no longer has a host.
about_author: Noor Crane is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent years cataloguing estate papers of families that preferred their histories sealed. They write horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the terrible intimacy of being remembered.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. During his overnight radio show, the first impossible call comes in: a listener who died six days ago, calm and specific, asking whether Isandro has 'found the door yet.' The beat is quiet dread — the professional composure of a man who trusts documentation beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Log
chapters.summary: Isandro reviews his station's caller logs and finds calls logged from numbers belonging to the recently dead, timestamps during hours the station was dark. His POV. Emotional beat: obsessive relief in evidence-gathering as a shield against belief.

chapters.title: Excavation at Ravensworth
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Marisol Vega, forewoman of the crew digging beneath the derelict Ravensworth estate for a new foundation. They strike not stone but lacquered wood — a door, its hinges rusted shut, sealed from the inside. Beat: unease disguised as professional pride.

chapters.title: Sealed From Within
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. An engineer confirms the bolts were thrown from the inside; there is no other exit from the chamber. One worker, Teo, jokes about knocking. That night everyone dreams of a hallway with their own name on a plaque. Beat: creeping violation.

chapters.title: Second Caller
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. A second dead caller, an old woman, describes the door precisely — down to the family crest scratched out — and says 'your grandmother threw those bolts, boy, and she used my hands to do it.' Beat: the horror becomes personal, hereditary.

chapters.title: The Estate Papers
chapters.summary: Isandro breaks into the boarded Ravensworth house and finds his great-grandmother Cordelia's journals: a ledger of names, faces surrendered across four generations, each entry ending with the phrase 'invited in willingly.' Beat: inheritance revealed as debt.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Cordelia's journal entries, presented as found text. The family summoned something during a famine winter to restore their fortunes; it takes identity instead of blood, wearing the surrendered until nothing original remains. Beat: complicity across generations.

chapters.title: Teo Knocks
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Against orders, Teo knocks on the door three times. Nothing happens — visibly. But at shift's end, Teo answers to his own name a half-second too slowly, and his reflection lags. Beat: dread through small wrongness.

chapters.title: The Face in the Booth
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Mid-broadcast, a caller breathes into the line, then speaks in Isandro's own voice. The station board lights up with calls from listeners who all describe seeing a man who looks exactly like him standing outside their windows. Beat: terror of being copied.

chapters.title: Quarantine of Hours
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The crew refuses to return; the site supervisor vanishes between his truck and the trailer, leaving footprints that end mid-stride. Marisol stays because her sister's name appears in a ledger page photographed on-site. Beat: guilt binding her to the danger.

chapters.title: Crossed Lines
chapters.summary: Isandro and Marisol connect when she calls the show anonymously and he recognizes the excavation sounds behind her voice. They compare notes: the door, the ledger, the lagging reflections. Beat: two loners choosing trust, fragile alliance formed.

chapters.title: The Middle of It
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Marisol returns to the site at dusk to photograph the ledger chamber; the door stands open. She is pulled — not physically, but attentionally — into the middle of it, hearing every stolen name speaking at once. Isandro, on air, hears her voice join the chorus of the dead. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: Held Until Sunrise
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He drives to the estate, barricades the broadcast equipment in the parlor, and keeps the show running as a lifeline — the dead callers guiding him through corridors that rearrange. Beat: desperate competence, prayer through documentation.

chapters.title: Wearing Isandro
chapters.summary: The double arrives at the house wearing Isandro's face and memories, pleading to be let in, reciting childhood details only he knows. Isandro documents the encounter aloud, broadcasting it, using the record as proof of which self is real. Beat: identity under siege.

chapters.title: Marisol Inside
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, from within. She moves through a hall of plaques bearing surrendered names and finds her sister's among them — taken years ago, unrecorded. She understands the thing hoards the forgotten. Beat: grief transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: The Bargain Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Isandro finds Cordelia's final entry: the entity can be uninvited only if the last Ravensworth voluntarily erases every record of himself — name, voice, archives — leaving nothing to wear. The dead callers confirm it, some begging him to do it, one begging him not to. Beat: the cost made explicit.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The house begins folding inward as dawn approaches; the entity grows frantic, offering Isandro restored versions of his dead parents if he lets it keep him. Marisol fights toward the parlor carrying the ledger. Beat: temptation at maximum pressure.

chapters.title: Erasure
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, climax. He burns the journals, deletes the archives, and speaks his own renunciation live on air — surrendering his name, his face, his documented self — while Marisol reads the counter-invocation from Cordelia's last page. The double unravels screaming in a voice that is and isn't his. Beat: sacrificial climax.

chapters.title: What the Door Kept
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. At first light the door is gone, replaced by solid earth, but the freed names rise like heat off the ground — her sister's among them, lingering long enough to be seen. Beat: catharsis, justice outside any law, grief given shape.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Epilogue-ish, Marisol's POV. Weeks later, the station runs an automated overnight feed; listeners swear the show still airs, hosted by a warm stranger whose name no one can recall afterward. Beat: haunting afterlife of the erased man.

chapters.title: The Unnamed Frequency
chapters.summary: Final chapter, omniscient drift. A new caller phones in — alive this time — asking about a door in her own family's cellar. Somewhere, something patient listens back. Beat: cyclical dread, the inheritance continues elsewhere.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Coda, Marisol's POV. She publishes the sanitized case file under Noor Crane's name, keeping one page back: a recording labeled only with a frequency, where a voice like no one's says goodnight to the city. Beat: mourning, memory, and the choice to remember what was erased.
